summary: An informational memo specifying an ATM-based protocol for communication between ST2+ agents, for the UNI 3.1 version.

plainLanguage.summary: How a special streaming protocol can ride on an ATM network.

questions: how does st2 work over atm networks
subtitle: A streaming protocol designed to work across ATM networks.

tldr.problem: ST2+ is a protocol for streaming data with guaranteed quality of service, but it was originally designed for IP networks. ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) is a different network technology that needed its own transport method for ST2+ streams.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies how to encapsulate ST2+ messages over ATM virtual circuits (VCs), and how ST2+ agents communicate using ATM's control and management planes to set up and tear down connections for streaming.
tldr.outcome: ST2+ can now work across both ATM and non-ATM networks together, allowing streams to traverse mixed network types while maintaining quality-of-service guarantees.

today: RFC 2383 is an Informational memo published in August 1998 and has not been updated or obsoleted. It describes a specific integration of ST2+ with 1990s ATM technology. Streaming protocols have evolved since then; the Integrated Services and RSVP (on which ST2+ was based) have seen limited deployment in general networks, though quality-of-service concepts remain important in specialized networks and modern frameworks like segment routing traffic engineering.

sections.title: Introduction to ST2+ over ATM
sections.content:
RFC 2383 specifies how ST2+, a protocol for streaming data with reserved network resources, can run on top of ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) networks. Rather than trying to run ST2+ directly as its own network, ST2+ uses ATM as a subnet technology—a carrier technology that handles the actual data transport.

The protocol does three main things. First, it specifies how ST2+ messages (called PDUs) get wrapped up and sent through ATM's forwarding mechanism. Second, it describes how the two protocols' control messages coordinate to set up and tear down connections. Third, it defines how ST2+ quality-of-service requirements map onto ATM traffic classes.

This design achieves several goals: it supports ST2+ streams that cross both ATM and non-ATM networks in the same path, it extends ATM's signaling to support features ST2+ needs (like negotiating the maximum message size at each hop), and it reduces some limitations in ATM's point-to-multipoint signaling.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of ST2+ as a shipping company and ATM as the truck they use. This memo shows how the shipping company can use the truck to deliver packages on time, and what kind of signals the company sends the truck driver.

sections.title: Protocol Architecture
sections.content:
The ST2+ over ATM architecture is organized into three communication planes, following the B-ISDN Protocol Reference Model. The user plane handles data: ST2+ data packets are wrapped in AAL5 (ATM Adaptation Layer 5) frames and sent over ATM cells. The management plane translates ST2+ quality-of-service requests—the promised bandwidth and delay characteristics—into ATM traffic-management parameters. The control plane handles connection setup: ST2+ control messages (called SCMP) are also sent via AAL5, and they coordinate with ATM's UNI 3.1 signaling to create and release virtual circuits (VCs).

The RFC specifies that each hop in an ST2+ stream corresponds to exactly one ATM virtual circuit. This one-to-one mapping means ST2+ does not try to multiplex many ST2+ hops onto a single ATM connection. The specification supports both permanent virtual circuits (PVCs, which are pre-configured) and switched virtual circuits (SVCs, which are set up dynamically on demand). For SVCs, the protocol supports several variants: the connection can be initiated from either the upstream or downstream end, and it can be point-to-point or point-to-multipoint.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a three-layer system: the top layer is the message you send (ST2+ data), the middle layer decides how fast it should go (management), and the bottom layer is the actual telephone call that carries it (ATM control). All three layers work together.

sections.title: ST2+ Messages and Flow Specifications
sections.content:
The RFC extends RFC 1819 (the base ST2+ specification) with new message formats. One key extension is the ST FlowSpec, which specifies the quality-of-service requirements for a stream. For controlled-load service (which promises reasonable performance), the FlowSpec carries a token bucket rate (the average bandwidth), a token bucket size (the burst size), a peak data rate, and minimum and maximum packet sizes. These parameters tell the ATM network how to reserve resources.

Another new element is the VC-type common SCMP element, which specifies what kind of ATM virtual circuit to use for this stream. It can indicate a PVC (pre-configured), a reused SVC channel, or a new SVC initiated from either end. This element also carries identifiers and IP addresses needed to coordinate the setup across intermediate ATM switches and endpoints.

The RFC notes several limitations of ATM that affected the design. ATM's standard signaling cannot negotiate the maximum message size at every hop, so ST2+ SCMP adds this feature. ATM in 1998 did not support different quality-of-service levels to different receivers on a multicast connection, so ST2+ applies its parameters uniformly or rejects the stream. Stream preemption (interrupting a stream to make room for a higher-priority one) is also not supported.
sections.plainLanguage: A FlowSpec is like a shipping contract: it says 'send 10 packages per second, but I can burst to 50 at once, and each package is at most 1500 bytes.' The VC type says which truck to use: a reserved truck, a borrowed truck, or a fresh truck ordered just now.

sections.title: Connection Setup and Operation
sections.content:
When an ST2+ agent wants to establish a stream, it sends a CONNECT message containing the FlowSpec and the desired VC type. If an SVC is chosen, the protocol then initiates ATM signaling (either from the upstream side or the downstream side, depending on configuration). ATM switches exchange SETUP and CONNECT ACKNOWLEDGE messages to reserve resources and establish the virtual circuit. Once the VC is ready, the ST2+ ACCEPT message flows back, confirming the negotiated parameters (especially the negotiated maximum message size).

To change flow parameters mid-stream, ST2+ sends a CHANGE message. However, the RFC notes that ATM UNI 3.1 (the version described in this memo) does not support changing QoS on an existing VC. ST2+ works around this by releasing the old VC and setting up a new one if a CHANGE affects all targets in the stream.

To tear down a stream, the protocol exchanges DISCONNECT and RELEASE messages between ST2+ agents and ATM switches, freeing the virtual circuit.

The RFC emphasizes that ST2+ and ATM are independent of routing and IP address resolution. It coexists with other protocols running on ATM, such as IPv4 encapsulation (RFC 1483), ATM ARP (RFC 1577), and NHRP (Next Hop Resolution Protocol).
sections.plainLanguage: Setting up a stream is like ordering a truck: send a request with your requirements, the truck company confirms they can do it, then you start sending packages. To change the deal in the middle, you have to order a new truck. When you are done, you release the truck.

sections.title: Status and Limitations
sections.content:
This memo describes the UNI 3.1 version of ST2+ over ATM. UNI (User-Network Interface) is the ATM standard for communication between customer equipment and the ATM network. UNI 3.1 is the earlier version; UNI 4.0 is a later version with more features. The RFC notes that a UNI 3.1/4.0 version would later add support for Guaranteed Service (a stricter quality-of-service model), LIJ (Leaf-Initiated Join, a way for new receivers to join a multicast stream after it starts), and other advanced features.

The specification does not require any changes to ATM standards themselves, and it does not specify IP address resolution protocols or routing—those are left to other specifications. The design is intentionally independent of router or switch architecture and of the core ATM NNI (Network-Network Interface) that connects switches to each other.
sections.plainLanguage: This describes how things work in 1998 with the ATM technology available then. Newer versions of ATM added more features, so the protocol was built to be extended later.
